newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: May Australian inflation expectations off slightly.
newsitem.headline: May Australian inflation expectations off slightly.

text.p: The Melbourne Institute survey of consumer inflationary expectations for May was down modestly at 3.4 percent from 3.5 percent the previous month.
The Insitute said that the modest decline was in line with the good underlying inflation performance seen in the first quarter CPI released last month.
Headline CPI inflation was 1.3 percent over the year, down from 1.5 percent in the previous quarter, while the underlying rate was unchanged at 2.1 percent.

"Over the past 12 months median expectations have come down 0.8 percentage points. As a consequence, inflationary expectations are now close to the lowest they have been since the survey began," the Institute said.

It said that it is likely that the measure of consumer inflationary expectations more closely reflects as 'underlying' inflation rate since individuals are simply asked whether or not they expect prices to rise.
As most consumers are unlikely to consider interest rates and/or rents a 'price' they most probably exclude these figures from their overall perception of future price changes.
Over the past five years, expectations have hovered around 4.0 percent. However, the past seven months have seen a significant downward shift, with expectations now close to 3.5 percent.

At 2.3 percent, consumers' median notion of current inflation is only marginally above the actual March quarter underlying figure, suggesting that consumers are relatively well informed about the current state of Australian inflation.
